items.item: mapInArrow and @arrow_udf (Spark 4.1) are two further Arrow-based entry points alongside the pandas UDF this topic measures — named in the syllabus clause directly but not independently timed, since the same batch-vs-row mechanism this topic already measures via pandas_udf applies to both.

at.out: mapInArrow and @arrow_udf named only in the syllabus mapping; not independently measured

items.item: The §2.1 cross-reference the syllabus clause names is this project's own earlier single-node topic on UDF optimizer opacity (scalar/table/aggregate UDFs blocking pushdown, costing and parallelism) — this topic is that same opacity cost, now specifically on a cluster crossing a process boundary rather than just blocking single-node rewrites.

at.out: the §2.1 cross-reference named only; that topic's own single-node opacity cost assumed, not re-taught

items.item: Arrow-optimised Python UDFs becoming default-on in Spark 4.2 (named in the syllabus clause) means a plain @udf-decorated scalar function can itself switch to Arrow transfer without being rewritten as a pandas UDF, on a recent enough Spark version — this topic's own examples.py targets 4.0.1, so its pickled measurement reflects the pre-4.2 default path deliberately, disclosed here rather than left ambiguous.

at.out: the Spark 4.2 default-on timeline named only; examples.py measures the pre-4.2 pickled default on 4.0.1

items.item: The pickled UDF path's per-row pickling cost (Pickler/Unpickler, net.razorvine.pickle) is a general-purpose Java object serialization library, not Spark's own Tungsten binary format — a second, separate overhead source layered on top of the process-boundary crossing itself, beyond what this topic's timing alone isolates.

at.step: Reveal: opaque, and pickled one row at a time

items.item: PYTHON_UDF_MAX_RECORDS_PER_BATCH, read directly in BatchEvalPythonExec.scala, controls how many rows Spark groups into one network round-trip to the Python worker even on the pickled path — the batching this topic's own Reveal step distinguishes is specifically the unit of work the Python-side loop processes (a row versus a whole Arrow batch), not the separate question of how many rows travel in one network message either way.

at.out: PYTHON_UDF_MAX_RECORDS_PER_BATCH named only; the per-row-vs-per-batch distinction this topic measures is about processing unit, not wire batching

items.item: A Python table-valued UDF (a Python UDTF, syllabus-named via the 'Python User-defined Table Functions' doc, one row in → many rows out) is a separate API shape from the scalar UDFs this topic measures, sharing the same opaque-to-Catalyst cost but not independently timed here.

at.out: Python UDTFs named via the source list; not independently measured, a separate API shape from the scalar UDFs this topic times

items.item: This topic's own measurement uses wall-clock timing (median of three repeated runs per path) rather than reading a cost from EXPLAIN FORMATTED's own plan text, unlike most of this chapter's other topics — necessary because the three-way speed gap is a runtime fact a static plan string can't show directly.

at.step: Reveal: the same computation, three real speeds

items.item: A UDF registered through spark.udf.register for use in raw SQL strings follows the identical pickled-or-Arrow cost model this topic measures for a DataFrame-API UDF — the registration mechanism changes how the function is invoked, not the serialization cost once it runs.

at.out: SQL-registered UDFs named only; the same cost model applies regardless of invocation mechanism

items.item: PYSPARK_PYTHON must point at an interpreter with pandas and pyarrow installed for the Arrow UDF path to run at all, independently of whichever interpreter launched the driver session — this topic's own examples.py disclosed this environment requirement directly, since the Python worker subprocess resolves its own interpreter separately from the driver's.

at.out: PYSPARK_PYTHON's own interpreter resolution named as a methodology note; not a syllabus claim

items.item: A pandas UDF's own batch size is governed by spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch (10,000 by default) — a separate config from the pickled path's PYTHON_UDF_MAX_RECORDS_PER_BATCH, so the two paths' own batching behaviour, while structurally similar, are tuned independently and don't share one config knob.

at.out: spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch named only; not independently measured or tuned here

items.item: Grouped-map and grouped-aggregate pandas UDFs (applyInPandas, a GROUPED_AGG pandas_udf) extend the same Arrow-batch mechanism this topic measures to a whole group of rows per key, rather than one flat column at a time — a different API shape built on the identical batch-crossing cost model, not independently measured here since this topic's own examples.py uses a plain SCALAR pandas UDF.

at.out: grouped-map/grouped-aggregate pandas UDFs named only; this topic measures the plain SCALAR case
